content:
Hoists can protect both the person and carers.

This guide covers the conversation. It is educational information, not a diagnosis or personal treatment plan.

Why a hoist

Lifting someone by hand can injure them and the carer.

Assessment and training

  • An occupational therapist assesses.
  • Carers need training before use.

Dignity

Involve the person in decisions.

Support for carers

Ask for a carer's assessment.

When to get help

  • Call 999 for chest pain, trouble breathing, signs of a stroke, or a fall with a possible serious injury.
  • Get urgent advice the same day (NHS 111 or your GP) for sudden confusion, a sudden drop in mobility, or a hot, swollen joint with fever.
  • See your GP for a steady decline over weeks, unplanned weight loss or repeated falls.

Never stop or change a prescribed medicine yourself. Ask your GP or pharmacist for a review.

Common questions

Where does the hoist come from?

Usually council equipment services.

Is it permanent?

Needs can change; ask for review.

Sources and further reading

  • NHS: Care services, equipment and care homes
  • NHS: Help and support for carers
  • GOV.UK: Apply for a needs assessment by social services

If you feel very unwell, call 999 or go to A&E. For urgent advice, contact NHS 111 (NHS 24 on 111 in Scotland; in Northern Ireland, your GP or GP out-of-hours service).
